subject: Business
title: The Jobs To Be Done Framework
description: A quick win: understand The Jobs To Be Done Framework.

hook.text: Nobody wants a quarter-inch drill. They want a quarter-inch hole. Theodore Levitt nailed it.

buildup.text: Jobs To Be Done says customers hire products to accomplish a specific job in their life.

discovery.text: A milkshake competes with bananas and boredom, not just other milkshakes. The job: make a long commute bearable.

twist.text: When you define competition by the job, your real competitors change completely — and so does your strategy.

climax.text: Clayton Christensen used JTBD to explain why innovations succeed or fail regardless of how good the product is.

punchline.text: Don't ask what your product does. Ask what job your customer needs done.

quiz.question: According to JTBD, what does a customer really buy?
options: A solution to a specific job they need done
The product with the most features

details.summary: Jobs to Be Done theory argues that customers hire products to complete specific jobs in their lives. Understanding the functional, emotional, and social jobs customers need done reveals opportunities that demographic segmentation misses, because the job defines the competitive set.
details.whyItMatters: JTBD shifts innovation focus from product features to customer progress. It reveals unexpected competitors doing the same job and uncovers unmet needs that surveys miss, making it one of the most powerful frameworks for product strategy.
takeaways: Customers hire products to make progress on specific jobs in their lives
The job defines the competitive set, not the product category
Functional, emotional, and social dimensions of each job must be addressed

faq.question: How is the milkshake example used to explain JTBD?
faq.answer: Christensen found that morning commuters hired milkshakes not for taste but for a filling, easy-to-consume breakfast that lasted their entire commute. The competitor was not other milkshakes but bananas, bagels, and boredom. The job was making the commute more interesting.

faq.question: How do you discover the jobs your customers are hiring products for?
faq.answer: Observe what customers actually do rather than what they say. Interview around specific purchase moments to understand the push away from current solutions and pull toward new ones. Look for workarounds and frustrations that reveal unmet jobs. Study non-consumption.
